_note: The decision core: name the message intent, then pick a ranked chart candidate. The Designer uses this at chart_spec time; the Auditor uses it to check the chart type matches the stated intent. Each candidate is tagged vega_lite_native: true (build it from vega_recipes.json) or false (build it from d3_fallback_recipes.json). DO NOT default to a chart because it looks impressive — pick from the message intent and the channel-accuracy hierarchy.
_sources: FT Visual Vocabulary (the 9-intent taxonomy + intent->chart method; re-authored, NOT FT prose). rohitg00/data-visualization (the purpose-first frame). Cleveland & McGill 1984 (channel-accuracy ordering). All re-authored.
how_to_use: 1. Say the ONE sentence the chart must make ('Argentina's win probability rose fastest in the last month').
2. Map that sentence to a purpose (comparison / composition / distribution / relationship / trend) — see purpose_first_frame.
3. Narrow the purpose to a precise INTENT below (e.g. trend -> change_over_time).
4. Read the ranked candidates; pick the first that fits the data shape and reader. Earlier = the FT/Pudding default for that intent.
5. Check the key variable lands in a high-accuracy channel (channel_accuracy_hierarchy).
6. If the pick is vega_lite_native:false, flag it for d3_fallback_recipes.json. Otherwise use vega_recipes.json.

purpose_first_frame._note: A coarse first cut from rohitg00/data-visualization. Pick the purpose, then jump to the precise intent. One sentence can have only one primary purpose — if it has two, it is two charts.
purpose_first_frame.comparison: Compare values across categories or items -> intents: ranking, magnitude, deviation.
purpose_first_frame.composition: Show parts of a whole, static or over time -> intents: part_to_whole, change_over_time (stacked).
purpose_first_frame.distribution: Show the spread/shape of one variable across many observations -> intent: distribution.
purpose_first_frame.relationship: Show how two (or three) variables move together -> intent: correlation.
purpose_first_frame.trend: Show change along time -> intent: change_over_time.
purpose_first_frame.spatial_or_flow: Geography -> intent: spatial. Movement/transfer between nodes -> intent: flow.

channel_accuracy_hierarchy._note: Cleveland & McGill 1984: how accurately the eye reads a quantity from each visual channel, most->least accurate. Encode the variable that MUST be read precisely in the highest channel the chart allows; use lower channels for secondary/categorical variables only.
rules: The number the reader must compare precisely -> position or length (bar, dot, line). This is why bars beat pie for comparison.
Angle/slope (pie, donut) reads worse than length — use pie only for a 2-3 slice part-to-whole, never for ranking.
Area (bubble, treemap) reads ~worse than length; acceptable for magnitude at a glance, not for precise comparison. Size by AREA not radius (encoding_craft.json).
Color hue carries CATEGORY (which group), color shade/saturation carries ORDERED magnitude (low->high). Never ask hue to carry precise quantity.
If two encodings disagree on importance, put the headline variable in the higher channel.

deviation.question: How far above/below a baseline, zero, or a reference is each item? (surplus/deficit, vs target, vs average, +/- change)

candidates.when: One value per category, signed; bars left/right (or up/down) of a zero line. The default.
Likert / sentiment: agree vs disagree stacked outward from a center.
Two opposing categories back-to-back from a central axis (e.g. men vs women).
Deviation over time; an area between the line and a baseline, colored by sign.

rules: Anchor on a zero (or explicit reference) line — see annotation_layers.json rule mark.
Use a diverging color scale (cross-ref design_tokens.json data_color_scales 'diverging'); positive vs negative must read instantly.

correlation.question: Do two (or three) variables move together? Is there a relationship?

candidates.when: Two quantitative variables, one point per observation. The default.
Add a third quantitative variable as point AREA (not radius).
Two variables traced over time — the path shows the trajectory (e.g. unemployment vs inflation by year).
Two related series on shared time but different units; layer a line over columns. CAUTION: dual y-axis implies false correlation — see encoding_craft.json dual_axis_warning.
Relationship between two CATEGORICAL/binned variables; cell color = count or value.

rules: Correlation is not causation — say so in the annotation, not the chart.
Add a trend/regression layer only if it aids reading; keep raw points visible.
Do not start a scatter axis at zero by default — see axis_label_polish.json scale.zero=false.

ranking.question: What is the order — who is highest/lowest, and by how much?

candidates.when: Rank by value; horizontal BAR when labels are long or there are many items. The default. Sort by value, not alphabetically (encoding_craft.json).
Rank many items compactly; one dot per item on a line — less ink than bars.
Ranked like a bar but de-cluttered: a thin stem + a dot; good when bars feel heavy.
Rank at two time points / two conditions — slope shows who rose and fell.
Rank where the magnitude gap is huge; symbol AREA per item, ordered.

rules: ALWAYS sort by the value (sort:'-x' or a field sort), never leave alphabetical.
Highlight the item the story is about with --accent; mute the rest (annotation_layers.json).
Truncating a ranked bar's baseline is dishonest — bars start at zero (axis_label_polish.json zero_baseline_rule).

distribution.question: What is the spread, shape, center, and outliers of one variable across many observations?

candidates.when: Shape of one continuous variable; bin + count. The default. Choose bin width deliberately.
Compare distributions across groups compactly (median, IQR, outliers). Vega-Lite has a native boxplot mark.
Show full density per group, not just quartiles. In Vega-Lite via a density transform + area mark (faceted) — heavier; use only if shape matters more than comparison.
Two back-to-back distributions (e.g. age by sex) — a spine of mirrored bars.
Small n — show every observation as a dot on a line; honest and uncluttered.
Show every observation with no overplotting; a jittered/offset strip. Strip is native; true beeswarm packing may need a D3 force — prefer strip first.
Emphasize percentiles / 'what share is below X' — a CDF line.

rules: Show the data, not just summary stats, when n is small (dot strip > box).
State the bin width / bandwidth; it changes the story.
Do not imply a smooth density from very few points.

change_over_time.question: How does a value change along time?

candidates.when: Continuous series over time, one or few groups. The default. Lines MAY truncate the y-axis (scale.zero=false) — they show change, not magnitude-from-zero.
Few discrete time periods where each period's MAGNITUDE matters; columns must start at zero.
One series where the magnitude/volume reads better filled; or stacked area for composition over time (watch occlusion).
Exactly two time points across many items — slope = who rose/fell.
A forecast with uncertainty: a central line + nested confidence bands (layer area bands by interval).
Time as the path between two variables (see correlation).
Daily values over months/years; a grid of day cells colored by value (rect mark over day-of-week x week-of-year).

rules: Label the line END instead of a legend when there are few series (annotation_layers.json text+argmax).
More than ~4-5 lines = spaghetti; switch to small multiples (vega_recipes.json facet) or highlight one + grey the rest.
Mark the key event/turning point with a rule + text (annotation_layers.json).

part_to_whole.question: How does the total break into parts? What share is each component?

candidates.when: Composition across a few categories or time periods; segments sum to the total. The default for >3 parts.
Compare composition across items where each is normalized to 100% — share, not absolute.
ONE total, 2-3 big slices, share is approximate. Use SPARINGLY — angle reads worse than length (channel hierarchy). Never for ranking or >4 slices.
Hierarchical part-to-whole with many items; nested rectangles by area. -> d3_fallback_recipes.json (Vega-Lite has no treemap layout).
How a starting total reaches an ending total via signed steps (bar mark with explicit y/y2 running sums).
A single share as a fraction of a ring; one number, decorative. Use rarely.

rules: If the reader must compare slice sizes precisely, use a bar, not a pie.
Order segments meaningfully (largest first, or a fixed semantic order), consistent across panels.
100%-stacked hides absolutes — pair with the total elsewhere if it matters.

magnitude.question: How big is each value, in absolute (not ranked, not part-of-whole) terms?

candidates.when: Compare absolute sizes across a few categories; vertical. The default. Starts at zero.
Same, horizontal — for long labels or many categories.
Two sub-values per category side by side (grouped); compare within and across (vega_recipes.json grouped).
Magnitude at a glance where exactness is secondary; circle AREA per item (not radius).
Counts as repeated icons (1 icon = N units); engaging, approximate. Repeat a shape/emoji mark.
Magnitude with less ink than bars; stem + dot.

One item's profile across ~4-8 comparable axes (e.g. a player's stats). Reads poorly for >1-2 series and exaggerates area — use sparingly; in Vega-Lite via polar/arc or a normalized line on a theta scale.

rules: Bars/columns MUST start at zero — see axis_label_polish.json zero_baseline_rule.
Size = AREA, never radius, for symbols (encoding_craft.json).
Avoid radar for precise comparison; the area is misleading.

spatial.question: Where — how does the value vary across geography?

candidates.when: A rate/density/normalized value per region; fill regions by a sequential or diverging scale. Vega-Lite geoshape OR Leaflet GeoJSON (component_implementations.json maps_leaflet). NOT for raw counts (area bias).
Absolute COUNTS by location; a sized circle (by area) per point/region centroid — avoids the choropleth area bias.
Movement between places (migration, trade) — curved/weighted lines between origins/destinations. -> d3 (geo + curves).
Show every unit as a dot to convey raw density without region shading.
Aggregate dense points into hex bins or density contours. Hexbin/contour generators -> d3.

rules: Choropleth needs a NORMALIZED value (rate, per-capita, density) — raw counts mislead because big regions dominate.
Prefer proportional symbols for counts.
Reuse ONE sequential scale (design_tokens.json) consistent with any bars/callouts of the same metric.
For interactive pan/zoom maps, Leaflet (maps_leaflet recipe) is usually the build.

flow.question: How do quantities move or transfer between nodes/states?

candidates.when: Flow volume between stages/categories; ribbon width = quantity. -> d3_fallback_recipes.json (d3-sankey).
Bidirectional flows among a fixed set of nodes around a circle. -> d3 (d3.chord).
Relationships/links among many entities; force-directed graph. -> d3 (d3-force). Also covers citation networks (component_implementations.json).
Sequential additive/subtractive flow to a total — the ONE native flow-ish chart (see part_to_whole).

rules: Most flow charts are NOT Vega-Lite-native — build with D3 and respect the SVG-mark ceiling (d3_fallback_recipes.json).
Flow diagrams get illegible fast — cap nodes/links, aggregate the long tail into 'other'.

native_false_index._note: Quick lookup of every candidate above tagged vega_lite_native:false — all route to d3_fallback_recipes.json.
